mainTopic: Items excluded from the oaths of שומרים, the rule that an oath needs a measured claim and a measured admission, and a lost מַשְׁכּוֹן
overview: This amud starts in the middle of a ברייתא that uses כלל ופרט וכלל to show that the laws of guardians cover only movable things that are worth money in themselves. That is why קרקעות, עבדים, שטרות and הקדש are left out, for a שומר חנם and for a שומר שכר alike. The גמרא then explains רבי מאיר in the משנה. He and the רבנן argue only about grapes that are ready to be picked, which רבי מאיר treats as if they were already picked. Next comes the rule that an oath is taken only on something measured. אביי says a claim of 'this house, full' would bring an oath, but רבא disagrees: both the claim and the admission must be measured by size, weight or number. A ברייתא backs רבא. The גמרא then asks why a large versus small מנורה brings no oath while ten versus five ליטרין does, and answers that a heavier מנורה can be scraped down to the lighter weight. A new משנה about a lost מַשְׁכּוֹן follows. It teaches that a full denial brings no oath and a partial admission does, and that the one who held the מַשְׁכּוֹן is the one who swears.

steps.title: The guardian verse covers only movable items worth money in themselves
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא reads the פסוק about a שומר חנם as a כלל ופרט וכלל. This limits the law to items like the examples: things that can be moved and that are worth money in themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If a man gives to his fellow' is a general statement. 'Silver or vessels' is a specific list. 'To guard' goes back to a general statement. When you have general, specific, general, you include only things that are like the specific list. Just as the list contains things that can be moved and that are worth money in themselves, so too the law covers anything that can be moved and is worth money in itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a ברייתא that shows where the פסוק teaches which items fall under the laws of a שומר חנם. It uses the method of כלל ופרט וכלל to set the limits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has a broad phrase, then specific examples, then another broad phrase. By the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל, the law reaches beyond the examples, but only to things that share their key features. The two features of 'silver or vessels' are that they can be moved and that the item itself is money's worth.

keyTerms.meaning: A general statement in a פסוק
A specific detail or list in a פסוק
A rule for reading a פסוק: include only things similar to the specific list
Something that can be moved
The item itself has money value

steps.confusionAlert: Don't confuse כלל ופרט וכלל with כלל ופרט (general followed only by specific). כלל ופרט by itself would limit the law to the exact items listed. כלל ופרט וכלל extends the law to anything similar to them.

phrases.english: 'If a man gives to his fellow' is a general statement,
'silver or vessels' is a specific detail,
'to guard' — it went back and made a general statement.
A general statement, a specific detail, and a general statement:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: you may only include things similar to the specific detail;
just as the specific detail is clearly
something movable whose body itself is money's worth,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל דָּבָר הַמִּטַּלְטֵל וְגוּפוֹ מָמוֹן.
phrases.english: so too anything movable whose body itself is money's worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ – כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא that the גמרא brought (just before this section) as the source for the משנה's list of items that are excluded from oaths.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The guardian laws apply only to items that are movable and worth money in themselves, learned through כלל ופרט וכלל.

steps.title: Land, slaves, documents and consecrated property are excluded
steps.stepSummary: Using the two features from step 1, the ברייתא excludes קרקעות, עבדים and שטרות. It excludes הקדש from the word 'his fellow.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Land is excluded because it cannot be moved. Slaves are excluded because the Torah compares them to land. Documents are excluded because, even though they can be moved, the paper itself is not money. Consecrated property is excluded because the פסוק says 'his fellow.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now applies its rule and lists exactly which items fall outside the guardian laws, with a reason for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each exclusion fails one test. Land fails 'movable.' Slaves fail because the Torah compares them to land. Documents fail 'worth money in itself,' since a שטר only proves a debt. הקדש is left out for a different reason: 'his fellow' means the owner must be a regular person, not the Temple.

keyTerms.meaning: Land
Canaanite slaves
Were compared (in the Torah) to something else
Legal documents, such as loan papers
Property consecrated to the Temple

steps.whatToRemember: Guardian laws apply only to movable items worth money in themselves, owned by a regular person. Land, slaves, documents and הקדש are therefore excluded.

phrases.english: Land is excluded, since it is not movable;
slaves are excluded, since they were compared to land;
documents are excluded,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּטַּלְטְלִין, אֵין גּוּפָן מָמוֹן;
phrases.english: since even though they are movable, their body is not money's worth;
phrases.notes: The paper is worth almost nothing. Its value is only in the debt it proves.

phrases.english: consecrated property — 'his fellow' is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule from step 1 to name the specific excluded items.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: קרקעות, עבדים, שטרות and הקדש fall outside the laws of a שומר.

steps.title: Where do we learn that a paid guardian does not pay for these items?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, that a שומר שכר does not pay for these items, and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says a paid guardian does not pay. From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and asks for its source. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 covered the פסוק about a שומר חנם, who swears. A שומר שכר appears in a different פסוק, and he normally pays for theft or loss. So the גמרא needs a separate source to show that these items are excluded for him too.

keyTerms.meaning: A paid guardian (שומר שכר)
From where do we know this?

phrases.english: A paid guardian does not pay.
phrases.notes: He means: he doesn't pay if one of these items is stolen or lost.

phrases.english: From where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the שומר חנם to the next line of the משנה about the שומר שכר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source showing that a שומר שכר does not pay for land, slaves, documents and הקדש.

steps.title: The same method applied to the paid guardian's verse
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא applies כלל ופרט וכלל to the פסוק about a שומר שכר and reaches the same list of exclusions.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'If a man gives to his fellow' is a general statement. 'A donkey or an ox or a sheep' is a specific list. 'Or any animal to guard' goes back to a general statement. General, specific, general, and so on, all the way to: consecrated property is excluded, because 'his fellow' is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. It runs the same reasoning from step 1 on the שומר שכר's פסוק and skips the repeated middle part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The specific list here is animals, which are also movable and worth money in themselves. So the exact same exclusions follow. The word 'כו׳' tells us to fill in the whole exclusion list from the first ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc.; the text is shortened here
Up to

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
'If a man gives to his fellow' is a general statement,
'a donkey or an ox or a sheep' is a specific detail,
'or any animal to guard' — it went back and made a general statement.
A general statement, a specific detail, and a general statement, etc.,
phrases.notes: Fill in the same reasoning and exclusions from the first ברייתא.

phrases.english: up to: consecrated property — 'his fellow' is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by repeating the method of steps 1–2 on a different פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The שומר שכר's פסוק also has a כלל ופרט וכלל, so the same items are excluded and he does not pay for them.
steps.whatToRemember: Both the שומר חנם and the שומר שכר have the same exclusions, each learned from its own פסוק by כלל ופרט וכלל.

steps.title: Quoting רבי מאיר: some things are like land and not like land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, where רבי מאיר says certain items look like land but are not treated like land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: there are things that are like land and are not like land, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's line in the משנה to set up a question about it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי מאיר says that certain things attached to the ground are not fully treated like land. The רבנן disagree. The 'כו׳' points us to the full case in the משנה, which is about vines.

keyTerms.meaning: Like land (in its legal status)

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
there are things that are like land
but are not like land, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ דְּבָרִים שֶׁהֵן כְּקַרְקַע וְאֵינָן כְּקַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר holds that some items attached to the ground are not treated fully like land.

steps.title: Why argue about vines full of fruit instead of empty vines?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if רבי מאיר holds that anything attached to the ground is not like land, the argument should have been about empty vines, not vines heavy with fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean רבי מאיר holds that anything attached to the ground is not like land? If so, instead of arguing about vines loaded with fruit, they should argue about vines with no fruit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the משנה placed the argument in the case of vines loaded with fruit. If רבי מאיר's view is broad, it should show up in a simpler case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי מאיר thought everything attached is not like land, the vine itself would not count as land. Then the argument would already exist over a bare vine. Choosing the fruit-laden case suggests his reason is narrower, so the גמרא pushes to understand his real reason.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication
Attached to the ground
Loaded (vines heavy with fruit)
Empty (vines with no fruit)

phrases.english: By implication, does Rabbi Meir hold:
anything attached to the ground is not like land?!
Instead of disagreeing about loaded vines,
let them disagree about empty vines!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the broad reading of רבי מאיר's statement quoted in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבי מאיר holds anything attached to the ground is not like land.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his view were that broad, the argument would show up even with fruitless vines. The משנה's choice of fruit-laden vines suggests a narrower reason.

steps.title: The argument is only about grapes ready to be picked
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא answers the question from step 6. רבי מאיר and the רבנן argue only about grapes that are ready to be harvested. רבי מאיר treats them as already picked, and the רבנן still treat them like land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא said: Here they argue about grapes that are ready to be picked. רבי מאיר holds they are like grapes already picked. The רבנן hold they are not like grapes already picked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6. It explains why the argument is about vines full of fruit and not about empty vines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 assumed that רבי מאיר says anything attached to the ground is not like land. This answer drops that idea. The whole argument is only about ripe grapes. Since they only need picking, רבי מאיר sees them as if they were already cut off, and the רבנן still see them as part of the land.

keyTerms.meaning: Grapes that are ripe and ready to be picked
They are treated like grapes that were already picked
They argue about

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי מאיר says that everything growing in the ground is like movable property. His view here applies only to fruit that is ready to be picked.

phrases.english: (Rather,) Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina said:
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in round brackets.

phrases.english: Here, they argue about grapes that are ready to be picked;
for Rabbi Meir holds: they are like grapes already picked,
and the Rabbis hold: they are not like grapes already picked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6 by narrowing what the argument is about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the argument is only about ripe grapes
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר holds that anything attached to the ground is not like land, so he should have argued even about empty vines.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees that attached things are like land. The argument is only about ripe grapes, which רבי מאיר treats as already picked.

steps.title: אביי limits the 'house full' case to an unspecified house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: an oath is only taken on something defined by measure or weight. אביי says this only applies when the claimant said 'a house' in general. If he said 'this house, full,' the claim is clear, and there is an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: We only swear on something measured by size or weight, etc. אביי said: This was only taught when he said to him 'a house' in general. But if he said 'this house, full,' his claim is known.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה. אביי adds a limit to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the claimant says 'I gave you a house full of produce,' and the defendant is exempt from an oath. אביי says the reason is that 'a house' is vague and has no clear amount. If the claimant points to a specific house, everyone knows how much is meant. Then the claim is clear enough to require an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Something defined by measure or weight
This was only taught when... (a phrase that limits a rule)
In general, without saying which one
His claim is known and clear

phrases.english: We only take an oath on something
that is measured by size or by weight, etc.
Abaye said: They only taught this
where he said to him 'a house' in general,
but if he said to him 'this house, full' –
his claim is known.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption in the 'house full' case applies only to a general house. A claim about a specific full house is clear and requires an oath.

steps.title: רבא asks why the משנה did not make אביי's distinction
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי. If 'this house' made a difference, the משנה should have split its own 'house full' case. Instead, it moved to a different case, 'up to the ledge' versus 'up to the window.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If so, the end of the משנה teaches: one says 'up to the ledge' and the other says 'up to the window,' and he is liable. Instead, it should have made a distinction within its own case: When is he exempt? With 'a house full.' But with 'this house, full,' he is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's limit by looking at how the משנה is worded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To show when an oath is required, the משנה used a new case, where both sides name a height in the house. רבא argues that if אביי were right, the משנה could have stayed with the same case and just added 'this house.' Since it did not, it seems that even 'this house, full' does not require an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Instead of teaching the last part of the משנה
Let it make a distinction within the same case
A ledge sticking out of the wall
When does this rule apply?

phrases.english: Rava said to him: If so,
instead of teaching in the last part of the mishna:
this one says 'up to the ledge'
and that one says 'up to the window' – he is liable;
let it distinguish and teach within the same case:
When is this said? With 'a house full,'
but with 'this house, full' – he is liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: אִי הָכִי, אַדְּתָנֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's limit from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that 'this house, full' is a clear claim that requires an oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If אביי were right, the משנה would have taught the difference inside its own 'house full' case. Using a different case shows that no such difference exists.

steps.title: רבא's rule: both claim and admission must be measured
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives his own explanation. There is only an oath when the claim is for a measured amount and the admission is also for a measured amount. This can be by size, weight, or number.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: He is never liable until the claimant claims something measured by size, weight, or number, and the defendant admits to something measured by size, weight, or number.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting אביי's view, רבא sets out the rule for when an oath is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, the problem in the משנה's 'house full' case is not whether the house is specific. The problem is that the amounts are not clearly measured. An oath needs a measured claim and also a measured admission.

keyTerms.meaning: He is never liable unless
That the claimant claims from him
And the defendant admits to him
Defined by number, by counting

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, an admission to part of a claim brings an oath only if both the claim and the admission are clearly measured amounts.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the condition for the oath of someone who admits part of a claim: both sides must speak about a defined amount.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
He is never liable unless he claims from him
something measured by size, by weight, or by number,
and the other admits to him something
measured by size, by weight, or by number.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: לְעוֹלָם אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיִּטְעָנֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's limit, which step 9 rejected, with רבא's own rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath is required only when both the claim and the admission are for something measured by size, weight, or number.

steps.title: A ברייתא supporting רבא: cases where there is no oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports רבא. It starts with cases where the defendant is exempt: he denies everything, or he admits to a small item when a large one was claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a ברייתא that matches רבא. If someone says, 'I have a כּוֹר of grain with you,' and the other says, 'You have nothing with me,' he is exempt. If he says, 'I have a large מנורה with you,' and the other says, 'I only have a small מנורה of yours,' he is exempt. The same is true of a large belt and a small belt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רבא's rule from step 10. This first part lists cases where the defendant does not have to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case he denies the whole claim, so there is no partial admission at all. In the מנורה and belt cases, 'large' and 'small' are not measured amounts, so the small item counts as a different object, not as part of the claim. That fits רבא's demand that both the claim and the admission be measured.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a ברייתא that agrees with him
A large measure of dry volume
Exempt (here, from taking an oath)
Candelabrum, lamp-stand
Belt
The other one (the defendant)

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא in line with רבא:
"I have a כּוֹר of grain in your hand,"
and the other one says, "You have nothing in my hand": he is exempt.
"I have a large menorah in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא מְנוֹרָה קְטַנָּה״ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: "You have only a small menorah in my hand": he is exempt.
"I have a large belt in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא אֲזוֹרָה קְטַנָּה״ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: "You have only a small belt in my hand": he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא as support for רבא's explanation in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that both the claim and the admission must be measured amounts.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing exempt and liable cases, ending with a general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Total denial, or admitting a 'small' item when a 'large' one was claimed, does not require an oath.

steps.title: Cases in the ברייתא where there is an oath
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If the claim and the admission are both measured (a כּוֹר versus a לֶתֶךְ, or 10 ליטרין versus 5 ליטרין), the defendant must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said, 'I have a כּוֹר of grain with you,' and the other says, 'I only have a לֶתֶךְ of yours,' he must swear. If he said, 'I have a 10-ליטרא מנורה with you,' and the other says, 'I only have a 5-ליטרא one of yours,' he must swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the opposite cases, where the defendant must take an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the admission is a measured part of a measured claim. Half a כּוֹר is part of a כּוֹר, and the מנורות are described by exact weight. Why a lighter מנורה counts as part of a heavier one, and is not a different object, is the question the גמרא takes up in steps 15–20.

keyTerms.meaning: Half a כּוֹר
ליטרא units, a measure of weight
Liable (here, to take an oath)

phrases.english: But if he said to him:
"I have a כּוֹר of grain in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא לֶתֶךְ״ – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and the other one says, "You have only a לֶתֶךְ in my hand": he is liable.
phrases.notes: A לֶתֶךְ is half a כּוֹר, so he admitted to a measured part of the claim.

phrases.aramaic: ״מְנוֹרָה בַּת עֶשֶׂר לִיטְרִין יֵשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ״,
phrases.english: "I have a menorah of ten ליטרין in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא בַּת חָמֵשׁ לִיטְרִין״ – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: "You have only one of five ליטרין in my hand": he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with the opposite cases, where there is an oath.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that both the claim and the admission must be measured amounts.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second half of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Admitting a measured part of a measured claim requires an oath.

steps.title: The ברייתא's general rule: measured claim and measured admission
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא sums up. There is never an oath unless the claim and the admission are both for something measured by size, weight, or number.
steps.simpleTranslation: The general rule is this: he never has to swear unless the claim is for something measured by size, weight, or number, and his admission is also for something measured by size, weight, or number.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא closes with a general rule that covers all of its cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This rule matches רבא's statement in step 10 almost word for word. Both the claim and the admission must be measured. Measuring only one side is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: The general rule of the matter
Something measured by size or volume
Measured by weight
Measured by number
And he admits to him

steps.whatToRemember: An oath is required only when both the claim and the admission are for a measured amount, by size, weight, or number.

phrases.english: The general rule of the matter:
he is never liable
unless the claimant claims from him
something measured by size, by weight, or by number,
and he admits to him
something measured by size, by weight, or by number.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the cases in the ברייתא with one general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no oath unless both the claim and the admission are for a measured amount.

steps.title: The general rule adds the case of 'this house, full'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the general rule adds. It answers with a rhetorical question: surely it comes to add 'this house, full,' teaching that this case also has no oath. That supports רבא over אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'the general rule' come to add? Is it not to add the case of 'this house, full'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its proof for רבא. It argues that the ברייתא's general rule exists to cover 'this house, full,' a claim that is not measured, so there is no oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8, אביי said that 'this house, full' is a clear claim and does require an oath. A general rule usually comes to add a case the ברייתא did not spell out. The likely added case is 'this house, full,' which the rule exempts because it is not measured, just as רבא said.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it come to add?
Is it not? (a question expecting 'yes')
'This house, full': a specific claim that has no measurement

steps.confusionAlert: 'This house, full' sounds very specific, which is why אביי treated it as a clear claim. The ברייתא's point is that 'specific' is not the same as 'measured,' and only a measured claim brings an oath.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא settles the dispute in favor of רבא: being specific is not enough, and the claim must be measured.

phrases.english: "The general rule of the matter": what does it come to add?
Is it not to add "this house, full"?
phrases.notes: This is the case from step 8. The rule exempts it, against אביי and in line with רבא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the ברייתא's general rule to complete the proof for רבא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that 'this house, full' does not require an oath, against אביי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra general rule at the end of the ברייתא, which must come to add a case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even 'this house, full' brings no oath, because it is not measured.

steps.title: Why is a large versus small menorah exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes the case of a large מנורה versus a small מנורה different, so that the defendant does not swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about a large מנורה and a small מנורה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts studying the ברייתא it just quoted. It asks why the defendant is exempt when the claim was a big מנורה and he admitted to a small one. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, claiming a large מנורה and admitting a small one means no oath. The גמרא wants the reason spelled out, because that reason will be tested against the 10-ליטרין case.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is different? (asking for the reason behind a distinction)
A candelabrum (a lamp-stand)

phrases.english: And what is different about
a large candelabrum and a small candelabrum?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מְנוֹרָה גְּדוֹלָה וּמְנוֹרָה קְטַנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from using the ברייתא as proof for רבא to analyzing the ברייתא's own internal logic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason a large versus small מנורה claim does not count as a partial admission.

steps.title: Because he admitted to a different object
steps.stepSummary: The answer: what was claimed was not admitted, and what was admitted was not claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What he claimed from him, he did not admit to; and what he admitted to, he did not claim from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason. The small מנורה is a totally different object from the big one, so the admission does not touch the claim at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath needs an admission to part of the claim. Here the defendant admitted to a different item entirely, so it counts as a full denial plus an unrelated admission. That means no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: He claimed from him
He admitted to him

phrases.english: That which he claimed from him, he did not admit to,
and that which he admitted to, he did not claim from him!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַה שֶּׁטְּעָנוֹ לֹא הוֹדָה לוֹ, וּמַה שֶּׁהוֹדָה לוֹ לֹא טְעָנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The small מנורה is a separate object from the large one, so there is no partial admission of the actual claim.

steps.title: Then the 10 versus 5 ליטרין case should also be exempt
steps.stepSummary: If that is the reason, a 10-ליטרין versus 5-ליטרין מנורה should also be exempt, yet the ברייתא requires an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, a 10-ליטרין and a 5-ליטרין מנורה too: what he claimed he did not admit, and what he admitted he did not claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. The same reasoning seems to apply to the ברייתא's other case, where the defendant must swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 5-ליטרין מנורה is also a different object from a 10-ליטרין מנורה. So by the reasoning of step 16, the ברייתא should exempt him. Yet in step 12 it said he must swear, which looks like a contradiction inside the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introducing a challenge built on what was just said)
One of ten (a מנורה weighing ten ליטרין)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two מנורה cases. Large versus small has no oath. A 10-ליטרין versus 5-ליטרין מנורה does have an oath. The question is why they are different.

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, בַּת עֶשֶׂר בַּת חָמֵשׁ נָמֵי –
phrases.english: If so, a ten-litra one and a five-litra one also:
that which he claimed from him, he did not admit to,
and that which he admitted to, he did not claim from him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בַּת עֶשֶׂר בַּת חָמֵשׁ נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the reason given in step 16 and applies it against the ברייתא's ruling in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that 10 versus 5 ליטרין requires an oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'different object' reasoning seems to apply equally to a lighter מנורה versus a heavier one, so both cases should be exempt.

steps.title: A menorah made of detachable segments
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר רב יצחק answers that the 10-ליטרין case is a מנורה built from pieces, so admitting 5 is admitting part of the same מנורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר רב יצחק said: Here we are dealing with a מנורה made of segments, so he is admitting to part of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר רב יצחק says the ברייתא's oath case is a special kind of מנורה made of pieces that come apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the מנורה is made of pieces, a 5-ליטרין portion really is part of the 10-ליטרין מנורה that was claimed. So it counts as a true partial admission, and an oath is required.

keyTerms.meaning: Segments or links that can be taken apart
We are dealing with (limiting a case to a specific situation)
From it, meaning part of it

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak said:
Here we are dealing with a candelabrum made of segments,
so that he is admitting to him part of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a מנורה built from separate segments.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A 5-ליטרין מנורה is a separate object from a 10-ליטרין one.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a segmented מנורה, the 5 ליטרין is part of the claimed 10, so it is a partial admission.

steps.title: The ברייתא does not deal with joined-piece cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that answer: if pieces counted, the ברייתא would have taught a belt of pieces too. Since it does not teach joined-piece cases, the מנורה is not one either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let it also teach a belt and explain it as made of joined pieces! Rather, it does not teach joined-piece cases. Here too, it does not teach a segmented case!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down רבי שמואל בר רב יצחק's answer. It shows that the ברייתא just does not deal with items made of pieces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the ברייתא a belt is listed among the exempt cases. If segmented items made an oath case, the ברייתא could have explained the belt that way too, as a long belt versus a short one made of links. Since it never does, the segmented מנורה reading does not fit the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: A belt
Made of pieces joined together
It teaches (the ברייתא states)

phrases.english: If so, let it also teach a belt,
and explain it as made of joined pieces!
Rather, it does not teach cases of joined pieces;

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי – בְּשֶׁל חֻלְיוֹת לָא קָתָנֵי!
phrases.english: here too, it does not teach a case of segments!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole segmented-מנורה reading of רבי שמואל בר רב יצחק.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא does not deal with items made of joined pieces, as shown by the belt, which it never lists that way.

steps.title: A menorah can be scraped down to five ליטרין
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר ממל explains that a מנורה is different: a 10-ליטרין one can be scraped down to 5 ליטרין, so the 5 is part of the 10.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי אבא בר ממל said: A מנורה is different, since one can scrape it and bring it down to five ליטרין.
steps.whatsHappening: After the first answer fails, רבי אבא בר ממל gives a new answer to the challenge of step 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Metal can be scraped away, so a 5-ליטרין מנורה can be made from the 10-ליטרין one. That makes the admitted 5 a real part of the claimed 10, so it is a partial admission and an oath is required. In the large versus small case no weight was named, so the small מנורה stays a different object, as step 16 said.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
Since, because
To scrape it (shave metal off it)
Litras, a unit of weight

steps.whatToRemember: A 10 versus 5 ליטרין מנורה is a partial admission, because the smaller weight can be made by scraping the larger one. A large versus small מנורה is two different objects, so there is no oath.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל:
phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Abba bar Memel said:
A candelabrum is different,
since one can scrape it
and bring it down to five litras.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל: שָׁאנֵי מְנוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 18 with a new answer to step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new explanation based on the physical nature of the item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A 5-ליטרין מנורה is a separate object from the claimed 10-ליטרין one.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 5 ליטרין can be made from the 10 by scraping, so it counts as part of the claim and an oath is required.

steps.title: Lost collateral: the lender claims, the borrower fully denies
steps.stepSummary: The lender says the loan was a סלע and the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth only a שקל, so the borrower still owes a שקל. The borrower says the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth a full סלע, so he owes nothing. The borrower is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone lent his friend money and took a מַשְׁכּוֹן, and the מַשְׁכּוֹן got lost. The lender says: 'I lent you a סלע on it, and it was only worth a שקל (so you still owe me a שקל).' The borrower says: 'No, you lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth a סלע (so we are even).' The borrower is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens with its first case. The lender demands a שקל, and the borrower denies owing anything at all, so the borrower is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree the loan was one סלע. The only fight is over the value of the lost מַשְׁכּוֹן. Since the borrower denies the whole claim and admits nothing, there is no partial admission, and so no oath is required.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה'; it marks the start of a new משנה
Collateral, an item the lender holds as security for the loan
A coin worth 4 דִּינָרִים
A coin worth half a סֶלַע (2 דִּינָרִים)
Exempt; here, he does not have to swear

steps.confusionAlert: Losing the מַשְׁכּוֹן cancels out the loan up to the מַשְׁכּוֹן's value. That is why the whole argument is about what the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth, not about the size of the loan, which both sides agree was a סלע.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who lends to his fellow on collateral
and the collateral was lost,
he said to him: "I lent you a sela on it
and it was worth a shekel,"
and the other says: "Not so,
rather, you lent me a sela on it
and it was worth a sela" — he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ עַל הַמַּשְׁכּוֹן וְאָבַד הַמַּשְׁכּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of the מנורה ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the borrower fully denies the lender's claim about the lost collateral's value, he is exempt from an oath.

steps.title: Lost collateral: the borrower admits part of the lender's claim
steps.stepSummary: Same claim by the lender, but now the borrower says the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth three דינרים. That means he admits owing one דינר out of the two that were claimed, so there is an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender says: 'I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a שקל.' The borrower says: 'No, you lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth three דינרים.' There is an obligation to swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה changes one detail from the first case. Now the borrower admits part of what is claimed, so an oath is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender claims 2 דינרים (4 minus the 2 the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth). The borrower's version leaves 1 דינר owed (4 minus 3). Admitting one out of the two claimed is a classic מוֹדֶה בְּמִקְצָת, which brings an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Silver coins; four of them make one סֶלַע
Obligated; here, obligated to take an oath
Admitting part of a claim, which requires an oath

phrases.english: "I lent you a sela on it,
and it was worth a shekel,"
and the other says: "Not so,
rather, you lent me a sela on it,
and it was worth three dinars" — there is liability.
phrases.notes: Three דינרים leaves one דינר owed, so he is admitting half of the שקל he was asked for.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 21: there was a full denial, and here there is a partial admission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the borrower admits part of the lender's claim (one דינר out of two), there is an oath.

steps.title: Reverse case: the borrower claims, the lender fully denies
steps.stepSummary: Now the borrower is the one making a claim. He says the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth two סלעים, so the lender owes him a סלע. The lender says it was worth just one סלע, so nobody owes anything. The lender is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower says: 'You lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth two (סלעים), so you owe me a סלע.' The lender says: 'No, I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a סלע.' The lender is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה flips the sides. Now the borrower demands money, and the lender denies all of it, so the lender is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth more than the loan, the borrower claims the extra סלע. The lender admits nothing, so this is a full denial with no partial admission, and therefore no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You lent me', spoken by the borrower
'I lent you', spoken by the lender

steps.confusionAlert: Watch who is speaking. In this case the first speaker says 'you lent me', so he is the borrower making the claim, and 'the other' is the lender.

phrases.english: "You lent me a sela on it
and it was worth two,"
phrases.notes: He means two סלעים, so the lender owes him back one סלע.

phrases.english: and the other says: "Not so,
rather, I lent you a sela on it
and it was worth a sela" — he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: סֶלַע הִלְוִיתַנִי עָלָיו וּשְׁתַּיִם הָיָה שָׁוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 21 with the roles switched: the borrower claims and the lender denies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lender fully denies the borrower's claim that the collateral was worth more, he is exempt.

steps.title: Reverse case: the lender admits part of the borrower's claim
steps.stepSummary: The borrower again claims the מַשְׁכּוֹן was worth two סלעים. The lender now says it was worth five דינרים, which means he admits owing one דינר out of the four claimed. There is an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower says: 'You lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth two (סלעים).' The lender says: 'No, I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth five דינרים.' There is an obligation to swear.
steps.whatsHappening: This mirrors step 22 with the sides switched. The lender admits part of the borrower's claim, so an oath is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower claims 4 דינרים (8 minus the 4-דינר loan). The lender's version leaves 1 דינר owed (5 minus 4). That is a partial admission, so there is an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Five דִּינָרִים, one more than a סֶלַע

steps.whatToRemember: The rule is the same in all four cases: a full denial means no oath, and admitting part of the claim means an oath. It does not matter whether the lender or the borrower is the one making the claim.

phrases.english: "You lent me a sela on it
and it was worth two,"
and the other says: "Not so,
rather, I lent you a sela on it
and it was worth five dinars" — there is liability.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 23 the same way step 22 contrasted with step 21: there, a full denial; here, a partial admission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lender admits part of the borrower's claim (one דינר out of four), there is an oath.

steps.title: Who takes the oath: the one who held the deposit
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that the oath is taken by the one who had the deposit in his hands, meaning the lender. The reason: if the other side swore, the holder might later bring out the deposit and show the oath was false.
steps.simpleTranslation: And who swears? The one who had the deposit with him. Because if this one (the borrower) swore, the other one might bring out the deposit (and prove him wrong).
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends by telling us which side takes the oath, and why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender held the מַשְׁכּוֹן, so he is the one who swears. If the borrower swore about its value, the lender could later produce the 'lost' item and show the oath was false. That would make the borrower's oath a false oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Takes an oath
A deposit; here it means the מַשְׁכּוֹן the lender was holding
Lest; out of concern that
And he will bring out (produce)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up who swears in the case of a lost מַשְׁכּוֹן, and the reason is a concern about a false oath.

phrases.english: And who takes the oath?
The one who has the deposit with him.
phrases.notes: That is the lender, who was holding the מַשְׁכּוֹן.

phrases.english: Lest this one swear,
and the other one produce the deposit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing when there is an oath (steps 22 and 24), the משנה tells us who takes it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The one who held the deposit (the lender) takes the oath, out of concern that if the other side swore, the holder might bring out the deposit and prove that oath false.
